column45: My job has played a big role in shaping my ability to innovate and think independently. Working with international clients, especially from Europe and America, has exposed me to higher standards, structured processes, and modern tools that are often missing in many local companies in Bangladesh. This environment encourages creativity, problem-solving, and accountability rather than simply following instructions.  In local companies, the focus can sometimes be more on short-term delivery and less on innovation or autonomy. But in my work, I’ve had the freedom to propose new ideas, improve workflows, and experiment with solutions that add real value for clients. This independence has not only improved my confidence but also given me a mindset where I look for long-term impact instead of just quick results.  Overall, my role has helped me bridge cultures and standards, learn from global best practices, and bring that knowledge back into my own work, something that sets me apart in the Bangladeshi job market.
column46: One big change that would help me be more creative and independent is financial security. In Bangladesh, most jobs don’t pay enough to allow true financial independence, which makes people focus more on survival than on innovation. If organizations here invested more in fair pay and long-term growth opportunities, employees could take risks, explore new ideas, and contribute beyond just meeting deadlines.  Another change would be giving employees more ownership and trust. In many local companies, decisions are often top-down, which limits creativity. On the other hand, when I’ve worked with clients from Europe and America, I’ve noticed they encourage open discussion, value individual input, and give space to experiment. Bringing that culture here would unlock a lot of hidden talent.
column47: I see my job as a stepping stone rather than a constraint. In a country like Bangladesh, financial stability is not something many of us are born into, it’s something we have to build slowly. There are always responsibilities and the pressure of taking care of family, which is deeply rooted in our culture. That makes it difficult to take big risks or fully dedicate yourself to groundbreaking innovation from the very start.  For me, a job provides the foundation, a way to gain stability, learn, and grow. Once that foundation is secure, it creates the space and confidence to pursue more independent and innovative paths. In that sense, my job isn’t just a paycheck; it’s a stepping stone toward the freedom to create something bigger in the future.
